title: Justice at the King's Tent
subtitle: Sher Shah’s Tent of Judgement
region: Delhi, Bihar, Punjab and the Sur provinces
moral: Justice must reach the weak or it is only display.

sources.note: Primary source for justice maxims, petitions, official punishments and collective responsibility.
Administrative parallels for official accountability under the later Mughals.

sources.citation: Muzaffar Alam, The Languages of Political Islam (2004); Satish Chandra, Medieval India, Part II (2007)
sources.note: Context for Indo-Persian kingship, justice ideals and administrative practice.

panels.shot: epic twilight wide of a royal campaign tent glowing in a dusty camp, low-angle

dialogue.text: In Sher Shah Suri’s war-torn age, the king’s battlefield tent becomes a court of justice—where a peasant may accuse a soldier, and the ruler’s mercy stands beside his power.

panels.shot: slow push-in from high bird’s-eye over North India, roads and rivers sketched across plains

dialogue.text: By the early 1540s, Sher Shah’s rule runs from Delhi to Bihar and towards Punjab, bound together by roads, serais and revenue officers—but power means little if the weak cannot find justice.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of the royal camp tent, lit by oil lamps, with Afghan nobles seated

dialogue.text: Abbas Khan Sarwani will later praise him: a ruler who hears petitions in camp and court, rebukes his own Afghans, and speaks of the oppressed as complainants before God.

panels.shot: close-up on Sher Shah’s face, stern eyes softened with attentiveness

dialogue.text: Indo-Persian ideals of kingship demand more than conquest: the just sultan must be a shadow of divine order, hearing the cry of the weak wherever his standard stands.

panels.shot: dramatic medium shot at tent entrance, a peasant steps forward toward the throne

dialogue.text: Sarwani’s stories show cultivators and traders walking into this tent of kings, naming the very officers who wronged them—and living to be heard.

panels.shot: medium shot with a burly Afghan soldier kneeling, guarded by other troops behind

dialogue.text: In one oft-retold pattern, an Afghan commander seizes a peasant’s land or extorts a trader; the complaint reaches the king, and the officer is disgraced or dismissed.

panels.shot: low-angle medium on Sher Shah rising from his seat, hand raised in admonition

dialogue.speaker: sher_shah_suri
dialogue.text: He who oppresses my subjects opposes God, and I will not shield him.

panels.shot: wide shot of a busy highway with serais, watchmen and distant hills

dialogue.text: Sher Shah’s new roads and serais promise safe passage from Bengal to the Indus—but every fresh path also invites robbery and abuse unless someone is made answerable.

panels.shot: medium shot at a village edge, headmen assembled before a royal officer with decree

dialogue.text: Sarwani records a harsher rule beneath the promise: if a traveller is robbed or killed near a settlement, the village headmen will answer with fines or worse.

panels.shot: interior medium shot in tent, Sher Shah listening to a merchant describe an ambush

dialogue.text: A merchant robbed on Sher Shah’s highway can appeal straight to the king; the story traces from road to pargana office to the village elder whose negligence is blamed.

panels.shot: medium shot of Sher Shah conferring with scribes and qazis over ledgers and reports

dialogue.text: Behind each anecdote lies a system: reports from highway posts, village fines entered into revenue records, and qazis and officials tying justice to the king’s communications network.

panels.shot: wide shot of a village assembly, elder kneeling as guards watch and villagers look on

dialogue.text: Collective responsibility forces local elites to police their own surroundings; it brings quick order to roads, but also spreads fear, as one man’s crime becomes the village’s burden.

panels.shot: moody interior shot of tent at night, Sher Shah alone, map and sword beside him

dialogue.text: For later writers, he becomes almost a saint of justice. Yet even Sarwani’s praise cannot hide the steel: his compassion travels with coercion in the same saddlebag.

panels.shot: solemn medium shot recalling a siege: distant fort of Raisen under smoky sky

dialogue.text: Elsewhere in this chapter stands Raisen, where Sher Shah’s siege ends in grim surrender and deaths; the same king who protects traders also compels Rajput forts to bow or break.

panels.shot: medium shot back in the tent, contrasting nobles on one side and common petitioners on other

dialogue.text: Justice at the king’s tent is never neutral ground: it balances the sword-bearing elite against tax-paying subjects, and every decision tightens or loosens that fragile bond.

panels.shot: wide shot of Sher Shah’s camp court, officers standing chastened as a peasant departs relieved

dialogue.text: For Abu’l-Fazl, writing later, real kingship demands such accountability: officers answer for abuses, roads are guarded, and royal authority rests on the trust of those who travel and sow.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on Sher Shah’s weathered hands resting on his knee, ring glinting softly

dialogue.text: Sher Shah’s justice tales are shaped by loyal chroniclers, but they reveal a hard lesson: power that travels in roads must also travel in responsibility—or it becomes only display.
